question: What is a pilot expected to do with en route, area, departure, arrival and aerodrome charts when planning an IFR flight?

options.text: Only read the weather information that the charts carry for each reporting point
Select routes, decode symbols and extract tracks, distances, altitudes and frequencies
Only check that the destination's runways are long enough for the planned landing mass
Plot the great-circle track by hand, because the charts show no airway routes

explanation: Charts are used to select routes, decode symbols, extract tracks, distances, altitudes, variation and navaid data, choose levels, complete the navigation log, identify airspace and extract approach minima.

question: Why must a pilot know the most common chart symbols and abbreviations before using a route manual in a timed situation?

options.text: The symbols change on every new edition of the chart
Looking every symbol up in the legend takes too long
The legend is not printed in the route manual at all
The abbreviations differ on every chart in the manual

explanation: The legend is available, but time is limited, so familiarity with the abbreviations, glossary and common symbols is needed to work efficiently.

question: What is aerodrome elevation?

options.text: The elevation of the threshold of the main instrument runway
The elevation of the highest point of the landing area
The average elevation of all the runways on the aerodrome
The elevation of the aerodrome reference point at the centre

explanation: Aerodrome elevation is the elevation of the highest point of the landing area.

question: What is altitude?

options.text: The vertical distance of a point on the earth's surface from mean sea level
The vertical distance of a level or point measured from mean sea level
A surface of constant pressure related to the 1013.2 hPa datum
The vertical distance of a level or point measured from a specified datum

explanation: Altitude is measured from mean sea level. Height is from a specified datum; elevation is for points on or fixed to the surface.

question: What is height?

options.text: A surface of constant atmospheric pressure related to the 1013.2 hPa pressure datum
The vertical distance of a level, point or object measured from mean sea level only
The vertical distance of a level, point or object measured from a specified datum
The vertical distance of a point on the earth's surface measured from mean sea level

explanation: Height is measured from a specified datum, such as the aerodrome or threshold.

question: What is elevation?

options.text: The vertical distance of a point on or affixed to the earth's surface from mean sea level
The vertical distance of a level or point measured from any specified datum
The vertical distance of an aircraft in flight measured from the threshold of the runway in use for landing
The vertical distance between two surfaces of constant atmospheric pressure

explanation: Elevation is used for points on, or fixed to, the surface of the earth, measured from mean sea level.

question: What is a flight level?

options.text: An altitude measured from mean sea level using the regional QNH set on the altimeter subscale by the pilot in flight
The lowest usable level above the transition altitude, allocated by air traffic control
A surface of constant pressure related to the 1013.2 hPa datum, separated from others by set pressure intervals
A height above the aerodrome measured with the QFE set on the altimeter subscale

explanation: A flight level is a surface of constant atmospheric pressure related to the 1013.2 hPa datum and separated from other such surfaces by specific pressure intervals.

question: What is the transition altitude?

options.text: The lowest flight level available for use above the transition layer, as allocated by ATC
The altitude at or below which vertical position is controlled by reference to altitudes
The airspace between the transition level and the transition height
The altitude above which aircraft must fly at flight levels on QNH

explanation: At or below the transition altitude the vertical position of the aircraft is controlled by reference to altitudes (QNH).

question: What is the transition level?

options.text: The level at which aircraft change from QFE to QNH on the approach
The highest altitude at which the regional QNH may still be used in the area concerned
The lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude
The airspace between the transition altitude and the cruising level

explanation: The transition level is the lowest flight level available above the transition altitude; it is usually allocated by ATC.

question: What is the transition layer?

options.text: The airspace between the transition altitude and the transition level
The airspace between the transition level and the lowest cruising level
The airspace between FL100 and FL245 in which levels change
The airspace between the aerodrome and the transition altitude

explanation: The transition layer lies between the transition altitude and the transition level.

question: What is the decision altitude or height (DA/H)?

options.text: The altitude or height on a non-precision approach below which descent may not be made without the visual reference required
The altitude or height at which the final approach segment of an instrument approach begins
The lowest altitude used to establish compliance with the obstacle clearance criteria for the procedure
The altitude or height on a precision approach at which a missed approach must be started without the required visual reference

explanation: DA/H is a specified altitude or height on a precision approach at which a missed approach must be initiated if the required visual reference has not been established.

question: To what is a decision altitude referenced, and to what a decision height?

options.text: Both to the threshold elevation
DA to mean sea level; DH to the threshold elevation
DA to the aerodrome elevation; DH to the touchdown zone
DA to the threshold; DH to mean sea level

explanation: Decision altitude is referenced to mean sea level (QNH) and decision height to the threshold elevation (QFE).

question: What is the minimum descent altitude or height (MDA/H)?

options.text: The altitude or height at which the glide path is intercepted at the final approach fix of a precision approach procedure
The lowest altitude allowed between radio fixes on an airway for obstacle clearance
The altitude or height on a non-precision or circling approach below which descent may not be made without visual reference
The altitude or height on a precision approach at which a missed approach must be started without visual reference

explanation: MDA/H applies to non-precision and circling approaches: below it, descent may not be made without visual reference.

question: What is the threshold?

options.text: The boundary between the taxiway and the runway
The point at which the ILS glide path meets the runway surface
The end of the runway available for the take-off run
The beginning of the part of the runway usable for landing

explanation: The threshold is the beginning of that portion of the runway usable for landing.

question: What is QFE?

options.text: The standard setting of 1013.2 hPa used above the transition altitude
The mean sea level pressure forecast for a region for the next hour
The altimeter subscale setting at which the altimeter shows elevation on the ground
The atmospheric pressure at aerodrome elevation, or at the runway threshold

explanation: QFE is the pressure at aerodrome elevation or runway threshold; with it set, the altimeter reads zero (height) on the runway.

question: What is QNH?

options.text: The atmospheric pressure at aerodrome elevation or the threshold
The height indicated on landing at an aerodrome with 1013.2 hPa set on the subscale
The altimeter subscale setting that gives elevation when on the ground
The mean of the pressures reported at all aerodromes in the region

explanation: QNH is the subscale setting at which the altimeter shows the aerodrome elevation on the ground, and altitude in flight.

question: What is the QNE value of an aerodrome?

options.text: The altimeter setting that makes the altimeter read zero on the runway
The difference in feet between the aerodrome's QNH and its QFE
The pressure at the aerodrome reduced to mean sea level in standard conditions
The height indicated on landing there with 1013.2 hPa set on the subscale

explanation: With 1013.2 hPa set, the altimeter on the ground shows the QNE value. It is used at some high aerodromes where the QFE would be outside the subscale range.

question: Why might the QNE value be used at some high-level aerodromes?

options.text: Their QNH is always exactly equal to 1013.2 hPa
Their altimeters are calibrated to a different atmosphere
Their QFE may be too low to set on the altimeter subscale
Their transition altitude is always at the aerodrome level

explanation: At high aerodromes the QFE may be so low that it is outside the limits of the subscale, so 1013.2 hPa is set and the QNE value used.

question: For what are most en route airway charts designed?

options.text: Airway instrument navigation with cockpit instruments, radio and ground-based aids
Planning of VFR flights below the lowest airway levels
Approach and landing at the aerodromes shown on the chart, using the minima printed on it
Visual navigation by reference to ground features, towns and roads

explanation: En route charts, mostly on a Lambert conformal conic projection, are designed primarily for airway instrument navigation using cockpit instruments, radio communications and ground-based navaids.

question: On en route charts, what does a shadow box round a navaid's identification indicate?

options.text: The navaid is a military aid not for civil use
The navaid is out of service until further notice
The navaid is associated with an airway or route
The navaid has a voice facility for ATIS

explanation: The shadow box is used when the navaid is associated with an airway or route. Off-airway navaids are unboxed, except that off-airway VORs are boxed outside the US and Canada.

question: A communication frequency is printed above a navaid's name on an en route chart. What does that show?

options.text: Voice communication is available through the navaid
The navaid is used for ATIS broadcasts only
The navaid is on a VHF channel in the 120 MHz band
The navaid's frequency is shared with the aerodrome tower frequency

explanation: Radio frequencies printed above the navaid name show that voice communication is available through that navaid.

question: On an en route chart, a communication frequency is printed as "2.35". What is the frequency?

options.text: 2.35 MHz

explanation: Frequencies in the 120 MHz range are shown without the "12", so 2.35 means 122.35 MHz.

question: A marine NDB is shown with "H + 04 & 15 (1)". When does it transmit?

options.text: At 04 and 15 minutes past each hour, for one hour each time it transmits
Every 4 minutes from 15 minutes past the hour, for 1 minute
From 4 minutes past the hour and every 15 minutes, for 1 minute each time
From 4 minutes to 15 minutes past each hour, on channel 1 only

explanation: The beacon begins at four minutes past the hour and then at 15-minute intervals, and each transmission lasts one minute.

question: On an en route chart, what is the difference between an LF bearing and a radial?

options.text: A bearing is true and a radial is grid north
A bearing is to the NDB; a radial is from the VOR
Both are measured from the station in degrees true
A bearing is from the NDB; a radial is to the VOR

explanation: LF (NDB) bearings are shown to the navaid; VOR radials are from the navaid.

question: In the US and Canada, what kind of airway has a designator starting with "V", such as V168?

options.text: A VFR corridor through controlled airspace below 3000 ft
A visual approach route to a major airport in the region
A VOR airway on the low level charts, below 18 000 ft MSL
A jet route for high performance aircraft above 18 000 ft MSL

explanation: Victor airways are VOR airways on US and Canadian low level charts, effective up to but not including 18 000 ft MSL.

question: In the US, between which levels are jet routes (such as J71) effective?

options.text: From 18 000 ft MSL up to FL450
From FL195 up to FL460
From 18 000 ft MSL with no upper limit
From FL245 up to FL660

explanation: Jet routes are for high performance aircraft, effective from 18 000 ft MSL to FL450 in the US (and to unlimited in Canada).

question: How are airways designated in European countries?

options.text: By the names of the two navaids at each end of the airway segment
By the letter V or J followed by a number, as in the US
By a phonetic alphabet letter and a number, such as A1 or B1
By a three-digit number only, such as 104

explanation: European countries use letters of the phonetic alphabet with a number, such as A1 or G27.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What is the minimum en route IFR altitude (MEA)?

options.text: The lowest altitude that gives obstacle clearance within 10 NM of the route centreline and its end fixes only, as derived by the chart maker
The altitude that clears all terrain within a latitude and longitude square by 1000 or 2000 ft
The highest altitude or flight level that may be used on an airway segment or route structure
The lowest published altitude between radio fixes meeting obstacle clearance and, in many countries, signal coverage needs

explanation: The MEA is the lowest published altitude between radio fixes that meets obstacle clearance requirements and in many countries assures navigation signal coverage. It applies to the whole width of the airway.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: Over what width does an MEA apply?

options.text: 22 NM from each of the VORs defining the segment
The entire width of the airway, segment or route between the fixes
The airway centreline only, between the two navaids
10 NM either side of the route centreline, whatever the airway width

explanation: The MEA applies to the entire width of the airway, segment or route between the radio fixes that define it.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What is the minimum obstruction clearance altitude (MOCA)?

options.text: The lowest altitude meeting obstacle clearance for the segment, with US signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR
The maximum usable altitude for a route segment, above which the airway structure does not exist at all
The altitude giving obstacle clearance within 10 NM of the route centreline, derived by the chart maker
The lowest altitude meeting obstacle clearance and navigation signal coverage over the whole segment

explanation: The MOCA meets obstacle clearance requirements for the whole segment but, in the US, assures navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: Within what distance of the route centreline does a route MORA give known obstacle clearance?

options.text: 10 NM
22 NM
25 NM
5 NM

explanation: A route MORA, an altitude derived by the chart maker, gives known obstacle clearance within 10 NM of the route centreline and end fixes.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What clearance does a grid MORA on an en route chart give?

options.text: 500 ft over flat terrain and 1000 ft over mountainous terrain above 3000 ft elevation
1000 ft everywhere, whatever the elevation of the highest point in the square
1000 ft where the highest elevation is 5000 ft or lower, 2000 ft where it is higher
2000 ft everywhere, whatever the elevation of the highest point in the square

explanation: Grid MORA clears all terrain and man-made structures by 1000 ft where the highest elevations are 5000 ft or lower, and by 2000 ft where they are 5001 ft or higher.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What does a grid MORA NOT provide?

options.text: Navaid signal or communication coverage
A value for each lat/long square
Clearance of the highest terrain
Clearance of man-made structures such as masts

explanation: Grid MORA gives terrain and structure clearance within its section but does not provide for navaid signal or communication coverage.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What does "Unsurveyed" in place of a grid MORA value mean?

options.text: The value is to be taken as 5000 ft
Flight is prohibited in that square at all times
The area has no terrain above 1000 ft
The information for that area is incomplete or insufficient

explanation: "Unsurveyed" is shown where information is incomplete or insufficient to set a value.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What does "+/-" after a grid MORA value indicate?

options.text: The value is in metres, not in feet
Doubtful accuracy, though believed to give sufficient clearance
The value applies to both VFR and IFR flights at all times of year
The value may be 1000 ft higher or lower in winter

explanation: Grid MORA values followed by +/- are of doubtful accuracy but believed to give sufficient reference point clearance.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: What is the maximum authorised altitude (MAA)?

options.text: The maximum usable altitude or flight level for an airspace structure or route segment
The altitude above which the transition level applies within a terminal area
The highest altitude at which an aircraft can maintain the airway centreline on one engine
The highest terrain or obstacle within 10 NM of the route centreline and its end fixes

explanation: MAA is a published altitude representing the maximum usable altitude or flight level for an airspace structure or route segment.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: On an en route chart, what does "E" by an airway direction arrow indicate?

options.text: Even levels are used in the arrow's direction, contrary to the semi-circular rule
Even and odd levels are both available in the direction of the arrow on the airway
The airway is for eastbound traffic only, at all levels
The airway is for emergency use only in that direction

explanation: E means even altitudes or levels in thousands of feet are used in the arrow's direction and odd in the opposite direction, contrary to the semi-circular rules.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: On an en route chart, what does "O" by an airway direction arrow indicate?

options.text: The airway is open only outside published military hours
The airway is an oceanic route outside radar coverage
Odd levels are used in the arrow's direction, on a one-way airway
Odd levels are used in both directions on a two-way airway at all times

explanation: O means odd altitudes or levels are used in the arrow's direction; it is used only on one-way airways.

subtopic: Minimum altitudes on en route charts
question: On an en route chart, what does "PPR" by an airway direction arrow mean?

options.text: Prior permission from ATC is required for flight in that direction
Position reports are required at every point in that direction
Propeller aircraft are permitted on the route in that direction
Preferred route for traffic to the nearest major airport in that direction

explanation: PPR means that prior permission is required from ATC for flight in the arrow's direction.

question: In which airspace class are only IFR flights permitted?

options.text: Class C
Class A
Class B
Class E

explanation: In class A only IFR flights are permitted; all are subject to ATC service and separated from each other.

question: In which airspace class are IFR and VFR flights permitted and all flights separated from each other?

options.text: Class A
Class C
Class D
Class B

explanation: In class B, IFR and VFR flights are permitted, all are subject to ATC service and all are separated from each other.

question: In class C airspace, from what are IFR flights separated?

options.text: From no other flights at all
From other IFR flights only, never from VFR flights
From other IFR flights and from VFR flights
From VFR flights only

explanation: In class C all flights receive ATC service; IFR flights are separated from other IFR flights and from VFR flights.

question: In class D airspace, what does an IFR flight receive in respect of VFR flights?

options.text: No air traffic service at all
Traffic information
Advisory service
Separation

explanation: In class D, IFR flights are separated from other IFR flights and receive traffic information on VFR flights; VFR flights receive traffic information on all other flights.

question: In class E airspace, which flights are subject to ATC service?

options.text: VFR flights only
IFR flights only
None of them
All flights

explanation: In class E, IFR flights are subject to ATC service and separated from other IFR flights; all flights receive traffic information as far as practicable.

question: In which airspace class do participating IFR flights receive an air traffic advisory service?

options.text: Class D
Class G
Class E
Class F

explanation: In class F, participating IFR flights receive an air traffic advisory service and all flights receive flight information service if requested.

question: What service do flights in class G airspace receive?

options.text: Separation of IFR from other IFR
Flight information service if requested
Traffic information on all flights as far as practicable
Air traffic advisory service for IFR

explanation: In class G, IFR and VFR flights are permitted and receive flight information service if requested.

question: Which airspace classes are controlled airspace?

options.text: A, C and E only
A, B, C, D and E
A to F
A, B, C and D only

explanation: Controlled airspace is airspace within which ATC service is provided in accordance with classes A, B, C, D and E.

question: Which of these is a function of an air traffic control service?

options.text: Issuing NOTAMs for unserviceable navigation aids
Calculating the fuel required for each flight in the area
Providing weather forecasts for the route ahead
Expediting and maintaining an orderly flow of air traffic

explanation: ATC service prevents collisions between aircraft and, on the manoeuvring area, between aircraft and obstructions, and expedites and maintains an orderly flow of traffic.

question: Unless stated otherwise, what is the width of an airway in the United Kingdom?

options.text: 5 NM either side of the centreline
2.5 NM either side of the centreline
10 NM either side of the centreline
4 NM either side of the centreline

explanation: An airway is 5 NM either side of a straight line joining each two consecutive points. Upper routes and advisory routes have no declared width but are deemed 5 NM either side for ATS purposes.

question: In the United Kingdom, what is the upper limit of lower ATS routes?

options.text: FL460
FL285
FL245
FL195

explanation: Lower ATS routes have an upper limit of FL245; upper ATS routes run from FL245 to FL460.

question: How can an advisory route be recognised from its designator?

options.text: Its designator ends with the letter R
Its designator ends with the letter D
Its designator begins with the letter A
Its designator begins with the letter U

explanation: The designator of an advisory route always ends with D, for example A1D or N562D.

question: In which airspace class are advisory routes in the United Kingdom?

options.text: Class G
Class D
Class A
Class F

explanation: Advisory routes are class F airspace, outside controlled airspace, along which an air traffic advisory service is available.

question: What does an air traffic advisory service aim to do?

options.text: Separate every aircraft, whether IFR or VFR
Give traffic information only when the pilot requests it
Keep IFR flights separated, so far as practical
Provide radar vectors to all VFR traffic

explanation: Air traffic advisory service, in advisory airspace, aims to ensure separation, so far as is practical, between aircraft operating on IFR flight plans.

question: What is a conditional route (CDR)?

options.text: A route for which a clearance is never needed
A route that may be flown only by military aircraft
A route usable only under specified conditions
A route that is closed during the summer period

explanation: Conditional routes are usable only under specified conditions, which are published.

question: How are upper ATS route designators shown in the United Kingdom?

options.text: Followed by the letter U, such as A1U or B40U
Preceded by the letter H, such as HA1 or HB40
Preceded by the letter U, such as UA1 or UB40
In lower case letters, such as ua1 or ub40

explanation: Upper ATS routes, FL245 to FL460, have designators preceded by U.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: When is generalised terrain shown on an area chart?

options.text: Always, on every area chart, for all terrain above 500 ft
When terrain within the chart rises more than 4000 ft above the main airport
Only on area charts for airports at an elevation above 5000 ft
When terrain within the chart rises more than 1000 ft above the main airport

explanation: Terrain may be shown on area charts when terrain within the coverage rises more than 4000 ft above the main airport.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What may be assumed where no terrain contours are shown on an area chart?

options.text: That the area has been surveyed and found clear of obstacles
That all terrain is at least 1000 ft below the minimum sector altitude
Nothing; their absence does not mean there is no terrain or structure
That there is no terrain or structure higher than the main airport

explanation: The absence of contours does not imply the absence of terrain or structures, and contours do not assure clearance. They do not replace the published minimum altitudes.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: How are SID and STAR charts drawn?

options.text: As diagrams that are not to scale
To the same scale as the area chart
At 1:500 000 like the VFR chart
To the scale of the approach chart

explanation: SID and STAR charts give a graphical, not-to-scale illustration of the prescribed procedures.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: Unless the chart says otherwise, what speed limit applies below FL100 on a typical departure or arrival?

options.text: 210 kt IAS
230 kt IAS
280 kt IAS
250 kt IAS

explanation: The usual speed limit is 250 kt IAS below FL100 unless otherwise cleared by ATC.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: On an arrival chart, what is an SLP?

options.text: A speed limiting point
A stop-line position
A sector level point
A standard landing point

explanation: SLP is a speed limiting point, from which the arrival speed limit applies.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: On a typical arrival, from when must the maximum arrival speed be kept?

options.text: From the transition level until landing, whatever the clearance
From 10 NM before the speed limiting point shown on the chart
From the top of descent until the outer marker on the final approach
From 3 minutes before the holding facility, or from the SLP shown

explanation: A typical instruction is to maintain maximum IAS 250 kt from a position 3 minutes before the holding facility, or from the SLP shown on the chart.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What are the standard maximum holding speeds above FL140 up to FL200, in normal conditions?

options.text: 240 kt
265 kt
230 kt
280 kt

explanation: Above FL140 to FL200 the standard holding speed is 240 kt in normal conditions; above FL200 to FL340 it is 265 kt, and above FL340 Mach 0.83.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is the standard maximum holding speed above FL340?

options.text: 265 kt
280 kt
Mach 0.80
Mach 0.83

explanation: Above FL340 the holding speed is Mach 0.83 in all conditions.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: In turbulent conditions between FL140 and FL340, what holding speed may be used?

options.text: 250 kt or Mach 0.74, whichever is more
280 kt or Mach 0.8, whichever is less
240 kt or Mach 0.78, whichever is more
265 kt or Mach 0.83, whichever is less

explanation: In turbulent conditions the holding speed is 280 kt or Mach 0.8, whichever is less.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is the minimum sector altitude (MSA) on an approach chart?

options.text: The lowest altitude at which the final approach may be started from the initial approach fix
The altitude at which the glide path is intercepted at the final approach fix
The altitude that guarantees reception of the navaid at any range up to 25 NM
An altitude giving 1000 ft obstacle clearance within 25 NM of the navaid, for emergency use

explanation: The MSA gives 1000 ft obstacle clearance within 25 NM (unless stated) of the facility. It is for emergency use and does not guarantee navaid reception; in sectors it becomes the minimum sector altitudes.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is the obstacle clearance altitude/height (OCA/H)?

options.text: The highest obstacle within 25 NM of the aerodrome plus a margin of 1000 ft above it for safety
The lowest altitude or height at which the aircraft may break cloud on a visual approach
The lowest altitude or height used to establish compliance with the obstacle clearance criteria
The altitude or height at which the ILS glide path crosses the threshold

explanation: OCA/H is the lowest altitude or height above the relevant threshold or aerodrome elevation used in establishing compliance with the obstacle clearance criteria.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: On an approach chart, what is the TCH?

options.text: The threshold crossing height of the glide path
The terminal control height for the TMA above the aerodrome
The touchdown zone height above sea level
The total climb height of the missed approach

explanation: TCH is the height at which the ILS glide path crosses the threshold.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: An approach chart shows "Rwy Elev: 3 hPa". How is this used?

options.text: Set 3 hPa on the subscale before landing
Add 3 hPa to the QNH to obtain the QFE
Add 3 hPa to the QFE to obtain the transition level
Subtract 3 hPa from the QNH to obtain the QFE

explanation: The runway elevation equals 3 hPa of pressure, about 90 ft. Subtracting it from the reported QNH gives the QFE.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is a non-precision approach?

options.text: An instrument approach using azimuth and glide path guidance
An approach flown visually after breaking cloud at the minimum sector altitude
An approach flown with the autopilot disconnected
An instrument approach without electronic glide path guidance

explanation: A non-precision approach, such as localiser only, VOR, NDB or VOR/DME, does not use electronic glide path guidance.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is a precision approach?

options.text: Any approach flown to a decision height below 500 ft
An approach to a runway with full approach lighting installed
An instrument approach using precision azimuth and glide path guidance
An instrument approach using distance information from a DME on the final segment

explanation: A precision approach uses precision azimuth and glide path guidance, such as ILS, MLS or precision approach radar.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is the missed approach point (MAPt)?

options.text: The point at or before which the missed approach must be started to ensure obstacle clearance
The point at which the missed approach holding pattern begins
The point at which the aircraft must have the runway in sight to continue the approach to a landing
The point at which the glide path is intercepted on the final approach

explanation: The MAPt is the point in an instrument approach procedure at or before which the missed approach must be initiated to ensure minimum obstacle clearance.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: An aircraft's approach speed (1.3 VSO) is 160 kt. In which approach category is it?

options.text: E
B
D
C

explanation: Category D covers 141 to 165 kt. Category C is 121–140 kt and E is 166–210 kt.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is the RVR?

options.text: The distance from the threshold to the point where the glide path touches down
The greatest distance at which prominent unlit objects can be seen by day from the control tower
The horizontal visibility reported by the meteorological observer at the aerodrome
The range over which a pilot on the runway centreline can see the runway markings or lights

explanation: Runway visual range is the range over which the pilot of an aircraft on the centreline can see the runway surface markings or the lights delineating the runway.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: What is visibility, in the aeronautical sense?

options.text: The vertical distance from the aircraft to the base of the lowest cloud layer
The distance a pilot on the runway centreline can see the runway lights or markings ahead of the aircraft
The ability, set by the atmosphere, to see and identify prominent unlit objects by day and lit objects by night
The distance at which the approach lights first become visible on final approach

explanation: Visibility is the ability, as determined by atmospheric conditions and expressed in units of distance, to see and identify prominent unlighted objects by day and lighted objects by night.

subtopic: Area, SID, STAR and approach charts
question: On an approach chart, what do "ALS out" and "TDZ or CL out" refer to?

options.text: Approach lights, and taxiway or car park lights, out of service
Altimeter setting, and terminal radar or communications, out of service
Airfield landing system, and the tower or control frequency, out of service
Approach lights, and touchdown zone or centreline lights, out of service

explanation: ALS out means the approach lights are out of service; TDZ or CL out means the touchdown zone or centreline lights are out.

question: An aircraft is on a 3° glide path at a ground speed of 150 kt. Approximately what rate of descent is needed?

options.text: About 1000 ft/min
About 450 ft/min
About 600 ft/min
About 800 ft/min

explanation: A 3° path is about 318 ft per NM. At 150 kt (2.5 NM/min) that is about 795 ft/min; the rule of thumb is five times the ground speed, 750 ft/min.

question: An aircraft is on a 3° glide path at a ground speed of 120 kt. Approximately what rate of descent is needed?

options.text: About 640 ft/min
About 360 ft/min
About 500 ft/min
About 900 ft/min

explanation: About 318 ft/NM × 2 NM/min ≈ 640 ft/min.

question: A departure requires a minimum climb gradient of 243 ft/NM. The ground speed is 240 kt. What rate of climb is needed?

options.text: 972 ft/min
1215 ft/min
583 ft/min
1458 ft/min

explanation: At 240 kt the aircraft covers 4 NM per minute: 243 × 4 = 972 ft/min.

question: A departure requires a minimum climb gradient of 243 ft/NM. The ground speed is 175 kt. What rate of climb is needed?

options.text: 709 ft/min
425 ft/min
850 ft/min
972 ft/min

explanation: Rate of climb = gradient × GS/60 = 243 × 175/60 = 709 ft/min.

question: A departure requires a 5.5% climb gradient. The ground speed is 230 kt. What rate of climb is needed?

options.text: About 1280 ft/min
About 760 ft/min
About 1530 ft/min
About 1265 ft/min

explanation: 5.5% of 6076 ft is 334 ft/NM. At 230 kt (3.83 NM/min) that is about 1280 ft/min.

question: About how many feet per nautical mile is a 4% climb gradient?

options.text: 318 ft/NM
400 ft/NM
243 ft/NM
152 ft/NM

explanation: 4% of 6076 ft is 243 ft per NM.

question: An aircraft is airborne at 0613 UTC and the ground distance to the first fix is 32 NM at a ground speed of 240 kt. What is the ETA at the fix?

options.text: 0617 UTC
0621 UTC
0619 UTC
0625 UTC

explanation: 240 kt is 4 NM per minute, so 32 NM takes 8 minutes: 0613 + 8 = 0621.

question: On a departure chart, what does "do not climb above the altitudes shown until cleared" mean for the SID altitude limits?

options.text: They may be exceeded once the aircraft is above the minimum sector altitude
They are minimum altitudes, which may always be exceeded
They may be exceeded only when specifically cleared by ATC
They apply only to propeller aircraft on the departure

explanation: The SID altitude limits are not to be exceeded until the aircraft is specifically cleared by ATC.

question: A noise abatement procedure requires crossing the monitoring point at not less than 1080 ft QNH. The aerodrome elevation is 80 ft. What height above the aerodrome is that?

options.text: 920 ft

explanation: 1080 − 80 = 1000 ft above aerodrome level (QFE).

question: On a holding pattern symbol, what does "D9" on the outbound leg mean?

options.text: The outbound leg is flown for 9 minutes
The outbound leg ends at 9 NM from the DME
The hold is 9 NM wide on the non-holding side
The ninth hold on the arrival route

explanation: D9 limits the outbound leg to a maximum of 9 NM from the DME.

question: On a holding pattern, what is the MHA?

options.text: The mean holding airspeed
The minimum holding altitude
The missed approach holding area
The maximum holding altitude

explanation: MHA is the minimum holding altitude for the pattern.

question: In the communications data on a chart, what does "G" next to a frequency mean?

options.text: Glider frequency only
Guard only (listening watch)
General aviation use only
Ground movement control frequency

explanation: G means guard only; X means on request, R radar capability, C clearance delivery and * part-time operation.

question: In the communications data on a chart, what does an asterisk (*) mean?

options.text: Radar service available
On request only
Emergency only
Part-time operation

explanation: The asterisk indicates part-time operation.

question: In the communications data on a chart, what does "X" next to a frequency mean?

options.text: On request
Radar available
Military use
Not in use

explanation: X means the frequency is available on request.

question: What is the common VHF emergency frequency?
explanation: 121.5 MHz is the international VHF emergency frequency (243.0 MHz is the UHF one).

question: What does "SSB" mean in the communications data for an HF station?

options.text: Standard service broadcast
Simplex short band
Secondary surveillance beacon
Single sideband

explanation: SSB is single sideband suppressed carrier HF communication.

question: On an en route chart, what does a semicircular "bypass" symbol at a reporting point show?

options.text: The point is a compulsory report for all routes
The point is a holding fix for every route passing through it
The point is outside controlled airspace
The point does not apply to a route that passes through it

explanation: A bypass symbol shows that a navaid or reporting point does not apply to a particular route passing through it.

question: An aircraft tracks 185°(M) on a heading of 180°(M) in airspace using semi-circular levels. Which levels should it fly?

options.text: Even levels
Odd levels
Any level it chooses
Odd levels plus 500 ft

explanation: Levels depend on magnetic track, not heading. 185°(M) is in the 180°–359° semicircle, so an IFR flight uses even levels.

question: An aircraft tracks 359°(M) on a heading of 010°(M) in upper airspace from FL245. What is its lowest available level?

options.text: FL290
FL250
FL270
FL260

explanation: The magnetic track 359° is in the westerly semicircle, so even levels apply; the lowest even level above FL245 is FL260.

question: Unless the chart says otherwise, how are tracks and courses on departure, arrival and approach charts given?

options.text: Grid
Magnetic
Compass
True

explanation: Courses on these charts are magnetic unless marked T (true) or G (grid).

question: Below an airway on an en route chart the figures "FL80 2700a" appear. What do they mean?

options.text: The MEA is FL80 and the route MORA is 2700 ft
The MORA is FL80 and the MEA is 2700 ft
The transition level is FL80 and the altitude 2700 ft
The maximum level is FL80 and the minimum is 2700 ft

explanation: The FL figure is the minimum en route altitude, expressed as a flight level; the figure followed by "a" is the route MORA in feet.
